newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's land prices fall for sixth year in a row.
newsitem.headline: Japan's land prices fall for sixth year in a row.

text.p: Land prices in Japan fell for the sixth straight year in 1996, with commercial land prices in city areas sliding over 10 percent from a year earlier, the government said on Monday.
But the news for the long-ailing market was not completely glum, with the tumble in prices smaller than in previous years.

The National Land Agency said prices of residential land were almost flat in major metropolitan areas, while the pace of decline in commercial real estate prices had been slowing since the latter half of last year.

In the three major metropolitan areas of Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya and their surrounding prefectures, the agency said commercial property prices declined 12 percent in 1996 compared with a fall of 16 percent the previous year.
Prices of residential land slipped nearly three percent cent, compared to a drop of five percent in 1995.
Japan's land prices tumbled dramatically since the heady days of ever-soaring property and stock prices in the late 1980s "bubble" economy.

The Land Agency data showed that since their peak in 1991, commercial land prices in central Tokyo have fallen 71 percent, while prices of residential property in major metropolitan areas have fallen 38 percent.
Analysts said the agency's data confirmed a growing distinction in prices between "good" and "bad" land, especially in central Tokyo.
"Prices of commercial property in attractive areas have bottomed out but prices of those that aren't in such areas are going to keep falling," said Hisanori Ito, an analyst at Nikko Research Center.

The data, which measured prices as of January 1, 1997, did not include a recent string of successful blue-chip property sales, which analysts say have given an important psychological boost to the market along with encouraging signs that the government has at last been spurred into action.

Sales in recent months of prime tracts of land once owned by the now defunct Japanese National Railways have attracted foreign buyers and fetched higher prices than expected, in one case nearly double the forecast price.

The government has also said it will draw up a scheme to boost liquidity in the land market by March 31. It is anxious to help the beleaguered banking sector, which is saddled with a mountain of bad loans, many of them made to the real estate sector and using property as collateral.
Analysts say the scheme, which will include plans to turn collaterised land into securities to be sold to investors, will act as a salve but not a cure-all of the land market's woes.
"Improving bad property is going to take a lot of time. I still expect central Tokyo commercial land prices to fall another seven percent this year," said Nikko Research's Ito.
